cue: How do you say someone is bursting with excitement?

es.meaning: To be so full of an emotion — usually joy or pride — that you cannot contain it.
es.example: No cabía en sí de orgullo cuando su hija subió al escenario.
es.exampleTranslation: He was bursting with pride when his daughter walked on stage.

it.literal: not to stay in one's skin any longer
it.meaning: To be unable to contain one's excitement or impatience.
it.example: Non sta più nella pelle: parte per il Giappone domani.
it.exampleTranslation: She can't sit still — she leaves for Japan tomorrow.

bridge.note: Both languages put the same picture on the page — a person too full of feeling for the body holding them — and then choose different containers. Italian names the skin, an outer wall the feeling is pressing against. Spanish names nothing at all: you simply do not fit inside yourself, the container left unspecified and therefore total. And there is a live wire underneath, because Spanish DOES have a skin version of this phrase, and it means something else entirely.

interference.es_to_it: Spanish supplies no skin to carry over, so the whole Italian phrase has to be learned as a unit — and note it stays in the negative: non stare PIÙ nella pelle, with più. Dropping it produces something that reads as a plain statement about location rather than the idiom.
interference.it_to_es: This is the dangerous direction. Translating the skin literally gives 'no caber en el pellejo' — which is real Spanish and means being OVERWEIGHT, not being excited. An Italian speaker describing a thrilled friend would be calling them fat. The Spanish idiom drops the skin entirely: no caber EN SÍ, usually with de + the emotion (de gozo, de contento, de orgullo).
